diagnostic_evidence.quote: We call \emph{eigenvalue trajectory} (respectively \emph{eigenpair trajectory}) any map $p\mapsto\lambda_p$ (respectively $p\mapsto(\lambda_p,\mathbf{x}_p)$) implicitly defined in \cref{eq:nlevp}.

issues.failure_explanation: A simple eigenvalue determines a unique local eigenvalue branch, but not a unique eigenvector branch: any nonvanishing continuous scalar multiple of an eigenvector trajectory is another trajectory under the paper's definition. No normalization or phase convention is imposed.

failure_location.quote: There exists a unique continuous eigenpair trajectory such that $\lambda(p^\star)=\lambda^\star$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State uniqueness only for the eigenvalue trajectory and state existence of a smooth eigenvector trajectory after imposing a local normalization and phase convention.
issues.overall_effect: The uniqueness assertion for eigenpair trajectories is false, although the existence and regularity conclusions can remain valid after choosing a normalization.
issues.title: Simple eigenvalues do not determine unique eigenpair trajectories
issues.why_classification: A short standard normalization correction preserves all substantive smoothness conclusions and later uses require only existence, not uniqueness.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Given a continuous eigenpair trajectory $p\mapsto(\lambda_p,\mathbf{x}_p)$, implicitly defined by a problem \cref{eq:nlevp} with $\mathbf{L}$ continuous in $p$, an exceptional point $p^\star$ is any point where $\lambda_p$ or $\mathbf{x}_p$ admit fewer continuous derivatives with respect to $p$ than $\mathbf{L}$ does.
A crossing point emerges at $\lambda=0$ for $p=0$, although eigenpair trajectories are smooth.

issues.failure_explanation: Under the given definition, the displayed smooth labeling has no exceptional point because neither eigenvalue nor eigenvector loses regularity. The proposed relabeled eigenpair maps do not repair this: their eigenvectors jump at zero and hence the maps are not continuous eigenpair trajectories, contrary to the definition's premise.

failure_location.quote: These points are exceptional because lack of smoothness may arise from a mislabeling of the eigenvalue curves.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either exclude removable smooth crossings from the definition of exceptional points, or introduce a separate labeling-dependent notion applying to continuous eigenvalue trajectories without asserting continuity of the displayed eigenvectors.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's classification of smooth crossings as exceptional points and its illustrative relabeling are mathematically inconsistent with its own definition.
issues.title: Smooth crossings are incompatible with the stated definition of exceptional point
issues.why_classification: The inconsistency is local to the terminology and example and can be corrected without changing the later bifurcation results.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Now, assume that $p\mapsto(\kappa_p,v_p,w_p)$ are all continuously differentiable at $p=p^\star$, so that the above formula holds there.

Letting $p\to p^\star$, the right-hand side above goes to zero since $\textup{Im}\left(\kappa_{p^\star}^2\right)=0$ and because the integral factor stays bounded as a consequence of the continuous differentiability of the eigenfunction trajectory near $p^\star$.

issues.failure_explanation: The contradiction assumes continuous differentiability through the exceptional point and uses bounded nearby derivatives. It therefore rules out a continuously differentiable extension, but it does not rule out a trajectory that is differentiable at the single point while its derivatives on the punctured neighborhood are unbounded or fail to converge.

failure_location.quote: Then $p=p^\star$ gives rise to an exceptional point, since the eigenpair trajectory is non-differentiable there.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace “non-differentiable” by “not continuously differentiable,” or add a nontrivial argument excluding pointwise differentiability despite the behavior of punctured-neighborhood derivatives.
issues.overall_effect: The asserted exceptional-point conclusion in the paper's sense remains supported, but the stronger statement that the derivative does not exist at the point, inherited by the corollary, is not proved.
issues.title: The bifurcation proof establishes failure of continuous differentiability, not nonexistence of a derivative
issues.why_classification: A local weakening preserves the theorem's substantive exceptional-point conclusion and all derivative-formula applications.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: From \cref{eq:integral}, one can easily prove (by expanding the square and exploiting the realness of Bessel functions for real inputs) that, for any $a,b>0$ and $c,d\in\mathbb{C}$,
Using \cref{eq:integral_sum} and simple changes of variables we compute

issues.failure_explanation: The proposition does not assume that $\kappa_p$ is real. Its proof substitutes Bessel functions evaluated at $\kappa_p\rho$ into an identity derived using real arguments and real-valued Bessel functions. For complex $\kappa_p$, a change of variables does not convert an integral of an absolute square into the displayed real-argument antiderivative, so the claimed boundary formula is not established in that regime.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the proposition and its proof to points or one-sided trajectory segments where $\kappa_p$ is real, or supply a different identity valid for complex Bessel arguments and absolute squares.
issues.overall_effect: The explicit boundary representation of the indicator is unreliable for non-real annulus trajectories; only its use on real branches is supported by the calculation.
issues.title: The annulus boundary formula is applied to non-real eigenvalues without a valid integral identity
issues.why_classification: The simplest repair excludes the paper's non-real spectral regime from the proposition, although the intended real-branch bifurcation application survives.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: If $p^\star$ is an order-$(1-\frac1M)$ root of $I$, i.e., $I(p)=(p-p^\star)^{1-1/M}\widetilde{I}(p)$ for some function $\widetilde{I}$ that is continuous and nonzero on a one-sided closed neighborhood of $p^\star$, then $p\mapsto\kappa_p$ displays a bifurcation of order $M$ at $p^\star$.
If the eigenvalue trajectory is purely real over a one-sided neighborhood of $p^\star$, then the converse is also true

issues.failure_explanation: The cited theorem gives sufficiency only when the zero has the specific fractional order $1-1/M$ (or satisfies its alternative factorization). Mere equality of the boundary norms says only that $I(p)=0$ and does not establish this root order. The theorem's converse makes the equality necessary for a bifurcation, not sufficient without the additional asymptotic hypothesis.

failure_location.quote: An immediate consequence is that, by \cref{cor:bifurc_sufficient}, a real (piecewise-smooth) eigenvalue trajectory undergoes bifurcation if and only if $\|v_p\|_{L^\infty(\partial B_1)}=r\|v_p\|_{L^\infty(\partial B_r)}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: State the boundary equality as necessary, and make sufficiency conditional on verifying one of the root-order or factorization assumptions in \cref{cor:bifurc_sufficient}.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised pointwise if-and-only-if diagnostic for annulus bifurcations is unsupported; a zero of the boundary expression may establish an exceptional point under other hypotheses but not necessarily an eigenvalue bifurcation.
issues.title: Vanishing of the annulus indicator is not by itself equivalent to bifurcation
issues.why_classification: The repair materially weakens a practical bifurcation criterion but leaves a comparable conditional criterion and the formal theorem intact.

issues.failure_explanation: Writing the radial amplitudes as $A_1$ and $A_r$, separability gives $\|v\|_{L^2(\partial B_1)}^2=a_m\pi|A_1|^2$ and $\|v\|_{L^2(\partial B_r)}^2=a_m\pi r|A_r|^2$. Thus $|A_1|=r|A_r|$ is equivalent to $\|v\|_{L^2(\partial B_1)}=\sqrt r\,\|v\|_{L^2(\partial B_r)}$, not equality of the two norms.

failure_location.quote: By the assumed polar-coordinate separability in \cref{eq:annulus:functions}, this is actually equivalent to $\|v_p\|_{L^2(\partial B_1)}=\|v_p\|_{L^2(\partial B_r)}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Insert the missing factor and state $\|v_p\|_{L^2(\partial B_1)}=\sqrt r\,\|v_p\|_{L^2(\partial B_r)}$.
issues.overall_effect: The alternative boundary-norm characterization is false for every $0<r<1$ except in degenerate zero-amplitude cases.
issues.title: The claimed equivalence with unweighted boundary L2 norms omits the inner-circle measure factor
issues.why_classification: This is a short local correction of the geometric measure factor and does not alter the underlying $L^\infty$ boundary criterion.
